title: Balak: how goodly are thy tents (Numbers 24:5)
hook: the curse becomes a blessing, and his words now open the morning service

segments.voice: Yesterday, three hilltops, twenty-one altars, and Balaam could speak only the word God put in his mouth. Your line was only the true word. Did you catch one pleasing thing that wasn't true? Day four hundred sixty-four.

Walk into almost any synagogue on a weekday morning, and the first words many people say as they come through the door are a line of Torah. It isn't from Moses, or David, or a prophet of Israel. It was first spoken by a foreign seer, hired by an enemy king, standing on a hill and trying to curse the people below. Balaam's third try, at Peor. He looks out over the camp of Israel, spread out tribe by tribe in the valley. And instead of a curse, these words come out.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS AT THE DOOR.` → `SPOKEN BY A HIRED SEER.` → `THE THIRD TRY, AT PEOR.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, the first two words are Mah tovu: how good. What did he see that was so good? The Talmud, and Rashi after it, give a surprising answer. Balaam saw that the entrances of their tents didn't face one another. Nobody could look straight into a neighbor's home. Living close together, they still gave each other privacy. That's the goodness he saw: not grandeur, but decency between neighbors. The Talmud also gives Balaam's blessings a darker reading. Rabbi Yochanan said, in paraphrase, from the blessings of that wicked man you can learn what curses he meant to say. And the rabbis later read tents and dwellings as the houses of prayer and study, the places Israel would gather. Then came the prayer book. Mah Tovu became the opening of the morning service, the verse said on entering the synagogue, followed by lines from the Psalms about coming into God's house. Not everyone was comfortable starting the day with Balaam. A sixteenth-century rabbi, Solomon Luria, is reported to have begun from the second verse instead, because the first came from Balaam's mouth. Most prayer books kept it anyway. There's something fitting about that. Words that were bought to curse, said by someone who'd rather not have said them, became the first thing many Jews say every morning. The blessing outlived the man and the money.
screen: `MAH TOVU: HOW GOODLY ARE THY TENTS.` · `DOORS THAT DIDN'T FACE EACH OTHER.` · `THE OPENING OF THE MORNING SERVICE.` · `A CURSE THAT BECAME A FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say Mah Tovu entering a room. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next room you'll walk into: your kitchen, your office, a classroom, a friend's home. If you pray, you can say, as you cross the threshold, the line from Numbers: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, thy dwellings, O Israel. If you don't, simply pause in the doorway for one breath and look for one good thing about the place and the people in it. Practice it now in your mind, then breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mah Tovu. How good. Balaam's blessing over Israel's tents, now the first words of the morning service.
Your line: how goodly are thy tents. Today, notice one way the people you live or work with give each other room, and thank them for it. Day four hundred sixty-four.

notes: Numbers 24:5 JPS 1917: confirm capitalization and punctuation ('How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!').
Solomon Luria (Maharshal) is reported in later sources to have begun Mah Tovu from the second verse because the first was Balaam's; confirm the attribution.
Sanhedrin 105b (Rabbi Yochanan: from Balaam's blessings learn his intended curses; all reverted except the synagogues and study houses); paraphrased only in part.
The hook says Balaam's third try was at Peor; the third oracle (24:3–9) follows Balak bringing him to the top of Peor (23:28). Confirm.
